item.title: Nvidia Brings Huang Back and Markets Roar, the Riemann Proof Passes Its Formal Check, and OpenAI's Chief Scientist Asks for Shared Limits
item.dc:creator: Varun Singla
item.description: Nvidia's board reinstates its founder, the Lean and Mathlib communities certify the Claude-assisted Riemann Hypothesis proof, Jakub Pachocki proposes industry limits tied to perplexity, a startup says AI agents designed…
item.content:encoded:
Nvidia's board reinstates its founder, the Lean and Mathlib communities certify the Claude-assisted Riemann Hypothesis proof, Jakub Pachocki proposes industry limits tied to perplexity, a startup says AI agents designed a new kind of CPU, Wells Fargo's agent-liability terms take effect, and FreeVideo runs a full video model on an 8 GB graphics card.

Viral / open-source spotlight

FreeVideo: a full video-generation model on an 8 GB graphics card

FreeVideo (github.com/FlashML-org/FreeVideo) is an open-source tool that generates video on an ordinary home computer. Its stated minimum is a graphics card with 8 GB of memory and 16 GB of system RAM, hardware that normally cannot hold a modern video model at all. It runs a model the project calls MiniMax H3, installs through a launcher on Windows, macOS or Linux, and plugs into ComfyUI, the popular node-based interface for image and video generation. One GitHub trend tracker listed it on November 22 at about 4,100 stars with roughly 400 added that day, among the fastest-growing AI repositories by share; another listing shows far fewer, so treat the count as approximate. Reports say the licence is Apache 2.0. The trick is memory juggling. The model is a stack of 50 large blocks, and only some fit on the card at once. Before each request a planner measures the machine and decides which blocks stay in graphics memory, which wait in ordinary RAM and which are streamed from disk when needed. It also picks compressed 8-bit weights suited to the card. It is like cooking a banquet in a small kitchen: you cannot lay out every ingredient, so you keep on the counter only what the current step needs and fetch the rest from the pantry. Why it is taking off: Video generation has been the one kind of AI that hobbyists could not run at home; it has meant paying per clip to a cloud service and accepting its content rules and queues. FreeVideo trades time for money: on a minimum machine it works, slowly and with heavy disk use, but it is private and has no per-clip fee. It fits the local-first pattern of recent spotlights such as Linger (Day 238) and Orkas (Day 234). The caveats: the 8 GB figure is the project's own claim, speed on small cards is poor by users' accounts, we could not verify the underlying model or its licence terms for commercial use, and cheap private video generation also makes convincing fake footage cheaper. Also trending: Claude-BugHunter, a bundle of security-testing skills for Claude Code, and autoclip, which cuts long videos into short clips.

Part 1Nvidia Reinstates Jensen Huang and Markets Rebound

On Monday, November 23, Nvidia's board voted unanimously to bring Jensen Huang back as president, chief executive and director, effective immediately. Colette Kress, interim chief executive since Huang resigned on November 12 (Day 230), returns to her job as chief financial officer, and Harvey Jones stays as board chair. It is a sharp reversal: on November 17 Jones had said the board did not intend to reinstate him. According to reports of the company's filing, the board said it had received input from senior levels of the US government and was confident the return poses no national security risk. Huang had stepped down after press reports about a personal relationship that US officials reportedly feared was tied to foreign intelligence. A committee of independent directors is still investigating what the board calls a foreign intelligence effort targeting Huang, and a new National Security and Export Control Committee will oversee trade compliance. President Trump said he had pressed for the return; Senator Warren said Nvidia still owes Congress answers, and three House committees still plan a closed-door interview with Huang on December 1. Nvidia shares rose about 31% to roughly $165, adding about $950 billion in value, the stock's best day since May 2003. The Nasdaq rose 6.5% and the S&P 500 4.7%, after a week in which the Nasdaq had fallen about 10% (Day 240). The concept, explained simply: Key-person risk is the danger that a company's value depends on one individual. Think of a restaurant famous for its chef: the building, the staff and the recipes are all still there if the chef leaves, but customers may not be. Monday's jump is that risk running backwards, a market paying nearly a trillion dollars for one person's return. The board's tool for handling the awkward part is an independent committee: a group of directors with no ties to management who investigate and report back, like asking a referee from another league to review a disputed call. Keeping that committee running while the person under review returns to work is unusual, and it is the detail to watch. Why it matters: Nvidia supplies most of the chips the AI industry runs on, so its leadership is everyone's supply-chain question. The episode also shows how closely government and the largest AI firms are now tied: a board cited government input in a decision about its own chief executive. A one-day rebound does not answer the questions from last week about borrowed money and circular financing; it only removes one source of doubt. The SEC inquiry (Day 239) and the congressional interest continue.

Part 2Lean and Mathlib Certify the Riemann Hypothesis Proof

Yesterday's open question was whether anyone independent would confirm that the formal statement in Levent Alpöge's archive really is the Riemann Hypothesis. That has now happened. The Lean and Mathlib communities published a joint statement, endorsed by the Lean Focused Research Organization and the Mathlib Initiative, saying they have full confidence in the result. They checked two things. First, that the theorem in Alpöge's library is exactly the definition called RiemannHypothesis in Mathlib, the community's shared library, which Lean experts and number theorists had vetted; two separate comparison tools reported an exact match. Second, that Lean's official kernel and several other independent proof checkers accept the exported proof. One report says a separate sandboxed rebuild reproduced all of the roughly 61.6 gigabytes of the published export. Some loose ends remain: one source says Andrew Sutherland's full end-to-end run at MIT was still listed as in progress, and outlets disagree on whether the result also covers the generalised version of the hypothesis. No expert has yet published a human-readable account of why the proof works.

The concept, explained simply: A proof checker earns trust by keeping the part you must trust very small. Lean's kernel is a short program that knows only the basic rules of logic. However huge the proof and whoever wrote it, human or AI, every step is reduced to those rules and replayed through the kernel. It is like a bank that does not care how clever your accountant is; it only checks that each line adds up. Running several different checkers, written by different people, guards against a bug in any one of them. The other half of trust is the statement: the comparison tools confirm the theorem proved is letter-for-letter the one mathematicians agreed on, so nobody has proved a look-alike.

Why it matters: This closes the gap we flagged on Day 240 between 'the file compiles' and 'it proves the right thing'. It does not close the second gap, understanding: a proof this large that nobody can read teaches little until people digest it. For everyday work the method is the lesson. Trust in AI output came here not from the model or its maker but from a small, independent checker and an agreed specification. Where you can build that pair, such as tests written before the code or a schema the output must satisfy, you can accept much larger pieces of AI work.

Part 3OpenAI's Chief Scientist Proposes Shared Limits on AI

On November 22 Jakub Pachocki, OpenAI's chief scientist, published an essay titled 'Perplexity and Intelligence'. He proposes an industry-wide standard that sets an initial limit on AI development and spells out the milestones developers must reach before the limit can be raised, with progress gated on how well humans can understand and monitor AI behaviour. Labs would agree on shared test methods and check one another's safety claims. He warns that AI could start speeding up training advances as early as 2027, faster than safety work can follow. Sam Altman endorsed the idea, writing that the industry should work toward agreement on common limits. The essay names no number, no auditor and no regulator, and Pachocki concedes the weaknesses: labs measure on different data, and some capability gains never show up in the metric. The context is OpenAI's own report of November 18, which estimated that its agents completed 46% of two-to-four-hour research tasks without help in October, up from 23% in March, while warning that researchers also changed which tasks they hand over. The concept, explained simply: Perplexity measures how surprised a language model is by real text. A model predicts the next word; if it is usually nearly right, its perplexity is low. Picture a guessing game: a perplexity of 10 means the model is, on average, as unsure as someone choosing between ten equally likely words, and a perplexity of 3 means only three. It is cheap to measure and hard to argue with, which is why it appeals as a shared speedometer. The weakness is that a speedometer does not tell you where the car can go. Tools, planning and longer reasoning can make a system far more capable without changing how well it predicts the next word.

Why it matters: A call for limits from the chief scientist of a leading lab, backed by its chief executive, is new. It moves the idea of capability thresholds (the Call for Control, Day 239) from outside critics to inside the industry. The test is whether a number, an independent measurer and a consequence follow; a limit that each lab measures on its own private data is a promise, not a standard. Any metric that becomes a target also tends to get gamed. Buyers should expect vendors' safety claims to start citing shared thresholds and should ask who measured them.

Part 4A Startup Says AI Agents Designed a New Kind of CPU

Architect Labs says its AI agents designed Frostbite, a general-purpose processor with its own instruction set, from start to finish. Instead of stepping through instructions as x86 and Arm chips do, Frostbite is built around interaction nets, a model in which a program is a graph and computing means rewriting connected pairs of nodes. The company claims 4.59 times the performance per watt of a conventional small in-order core, averaged over 25 workloads such as matrix multiplication, JSON parsing and decompression, and about 8.8 times the performance per unit of chip area. The detail worth reading: the gain was 6.02 times on the 10 workloads the agents saw while designing and 3.83 times on the 15 held back until the end. All of it comes from simulation; no chip has been made. The comparison core is not named, existing software will not run without being rewritten for the new model, and nobody outside the company has reproduced the numbers.

The concept, explained simply: A held-out set is a batch of tests the designer is not allowed to see until the work is finished, like an exam paper kept sealed while you revise from past papers. Scores on the past papers show how well you learned those questions; the sealed paper shows whether you learned the subject. A drop from 6.02 to 3.83 is the usual sign of some tuning to the practice set, though 3.83 would still be a large gain. Pre-silicon means the figures come from a software model of the chip. Real silicon adds heat, wiring delay and manufacturing limits, which usually shrink such numbers.

Why it matters: After the Riemann proof, this is a second claim in a week that AI agents did open-ended technical design rather than assist with it. It is far less verified: one is certified by an independent checker, the other rests on the company's own simulator and an unnamed baseline. Use the same questions for any 'AI designed X' headline: was there a held-out test, who chose the baseline, and has anyone else reproduced it? It also connects to section 3, since AI designing better chips for AI is one of the feedback loops Pachocki worries about.

Part 5Wells Fargo's AI-Agent Terms Put the Risk on Customers

Wells Fargo's updated Online Access Agreement takes effect today, November 24, with a new section on third-party AI agents. According to press coverage (we could not open the agreement itself), a customer who lets an agent into their account is responsible for what it does, including unintended actions, mistakes in interpreting instructions, cases where the agent goes beyond the authority it was given, and actions caused by manipulated inputs, which would cover prompt injection. Customers who cut off an agent must keep evidence that they did so and show it to the bank on request. The bank may require agents to be registered and may block them, and the terms apply subject to applicable law. Other large banks have gone the other way: Citi says it does not allow third-party agents to log in or transact at all, and several others restrict them. The concept, explained simply: This is about who pays when a delegate gets it wrong. US rules on electronic payments protect you when a stranger takes money from your account, but if you hand someone your card and PIN, what they do generally counts as authorised by you until you tell the bank otherwise. Wells Fargo is treating an AI agent the same way: like a house-sitter you gave the keys to. If the house-sitter is tricked into letting a burglar in, the first question is why they had the keys. The requirement to prove revocation adds a practical twist: taking the keys back counts only if you can show when you did it. Why it matters: On Day 231 we covered websites locking agents out; this is the other route, letting them in and moving the risk to the user. It sets a likely template for banks, brokers and retailers ahead of an agent-driven holiday shopping season. For anyone using a personal agent with payment access, prompt injection is now a personal financial risk, not just a vendor's security problem. Spending limits, confirmation steps and tokenised cards (the ChatGPT Wallet, Day 232; Walmart's gateway, Day 239) matter more as a result. Whether such terms hold up against consumer-protection law is untested.

Market signal

The signal is that confidence in AI still hangs on very few points of trust. One person's return moved Nvidia by nearly a trillion dollars in a day and lifted the whole Nasdaq. One small kernel turned an unreadable 61-gigabyte proof into an accepted result. One proposed number, not yet chosen, is being offered as the industry's brake. And one contract clause decides who pays when an agent is fooled. Expect boards and investors to price key-person risk at AI firms more explicitly, independent verification to become a selling point for AI results, and liability terms for agents to spread from banks to every consumer platform before the rules are tested in court.

Practical takeaways
Name your key people and their backups.

List the individuals and single suppliers your AI plans depend on, and write down what you would do in the first week without each.

Pair AI output with a small independent checker.

Where you can, fix a specification first (tests, a schema, a formal statement) and accept AI work only when a separate tool confirms it meets that specification.

Check the statement, not only the proof.

When a result is called verified, confirm that what was checked is exactly what you asked for, not a close relative.

Ask for the held-out score.

For any benchmark claim, ask which tests the system saw during development and what it scored on the ones it did not.

Ask who measured the safety threshold.

When a vendor cites a capability or safety limit, find out whether the measurement was its own or an outside party's.

Read the agent clause before you connect an agent.

Before giving a personal AI agent access to a bank, broker or shop, read the provider's terms on who is liable for its actions.

Keep proof when you revoke an agent's access.

Save a dated screenshot or confirmation e-mail whenever you remove an agent's permissions, and tell the provider in writing.

Cap what an agent can spend.

Use a tokenised or virtual card with a low limit and require confirmation for payments, so a tricked agent cannot do much damage.

Self-test
What is key-person risk, and how did Nvidia's share price show it on November 23?

It is the danger that a company's value depends on one individual; Nvidia gained about 31%, roughly $950 billion, on the day its founder was reinstated.

What two things did the Lean and Mathlib communities check about the Riemann Hypothesis proof?

That the theorem proved exactly matches Mathlib's agreed statement of the hypothesis, and that Lean's kernel and other independent checkers accept the proof.

What does perplexity measure, and why is it an incomplete limit on AI capability?

It measures how surprised a model is by real text, that is, how well it predicts the next word; tools, planning and reasoning can add capability without lowering it.

Frostbite scored 6.02 times on ten workloads and 3.83 times on fifteen others. What does the gap suggest?

The ten were used during design and the fifteen were held out, so the gap suggests some tuning to the practice set; the held-out figure is the more honest one.

Under Wells Fargo's new terms, who is responsible if a customer's AI agent is tricked by a prompt injection?

The customer, according to press reports of the agreement, until the bank has been told the agent's access is revoked and the customer can prove it.

How does FreeVideo fit a large video model onto an 8 GB graphics card?

A planner keeps only some of the model's blocks in graphics memory at a time, holding the rest in system RAM or streaming them from disk, and uses compressed 8-bit weights.

What we're watching

Whether Nvidia's rally holds on Tuesday, and what the independent committee and the December 1 House interview with Huang produce. What We're Watching: Andrew Sutherland's end-to-end check of the Riemann proof, a ruling on whether it covers the generalised hypothesis, and the first human-readable account from number theorists. What We're Watching: Whether Anthropic, Google DeepMind or regulators respond to Pachocki's proposal, and whether anyone names a number or an independent measurer. What We're Watching: Any outside reproduction of Architect Labs' Frostbite results, or the name of the baseline core. What We're Watching: Whether other banks copy Wells Fargo's agent clause, the first disputes under it, and Black Friday data on agent-driven shopping.

Sources. axios.com, cnn.com, cbsnews.com, nbcnews.com, sec.gov and nvidianews.nvidia.com (Huang's reinstatement, as reported); finance.yahoo.com, cnbc.com, kiplinger.com, benzinga.com and investing.com (market figures); leanprover-community.github.io, the-decoder.com, scientificamerican.com and mlq.ai (Lean and Mathlib certification); thenextweb.com, theprint.in, news.bloomberglaw.com, snowrock.com and ppc.land (Pachocki's essay, OpenAI's research-task figures); hwbusters.com, notebookcheck.net, marktechpost.com and i10x.ai (Frostbite); americanbanker.com, acainternational.org, accountsrecovery.net and cutoday.info (Wells Fargo terms); github.com/FlashML-org/FreeVideo, alphasignal.ai and github.com/Chestnuts-Sisyphus/gittok (FreeVideo and trending lists). Figures are secondary reports and unverified unless from the company's own page or filing.

item.title: A Claimed AI Proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, a Coding Agent That Committed the Keys, and the AI Trade's Worst Week
item.dc:creator: Varun Singla
item.description: An Anthropic mathematician's Claude-assisted, machine-checked proof claim, Together AI's prompt leak and OpenRouter's purge of three providers, a market correction led by AI stocks, the governors' plan to share AI…
item.content:encoded:
An Anthropic mathematician's Claude-assisted, machine-checked proof claim, Together AI's prompt leak and OpenRouter's purge of three providers, a market correction led by AI stocks, the governors' plan to share AI rule-making with Washington, stalled UN talks on autonomous weapons, and LoopForge, Tencent's workflow engine that puts human approval gates around coding agents.

Viral / open-source spotlight

LoopForge: Tencent's workflow engine that puts approval gates around coding agents

LoopForge (github.com/Tencent/LoopForge) is a self-hosted workspace from Tencent for shipping software with coding agents. It has been appearing on GitHub trending lists this week, with about 5,400 stars according to one tracker and releases up to v0.3.6. It does not replace Claude Code, Codex or Tencent's own CodeBuddy; it orchestrates them. A team writes a standard operating procedure, a fixed workflow that mixes three kinds of step: agent steps (implement, review), deterministic scripts (run the tests, build) and human approval gates, where the run pauses until a person approves it or sends the work back to a chosen step. Work runs in Docker sandboxes against real repositories, results can be delivered as GitHub pull requests, and each run keeps its evidence. A blog reports an MIT licence, which we did not verify. Why it is taking off: Teams have learned that the hard part of coding agents is not getting code written but trusting what comes out. Today's Together AI story is the cautionary tale: an agent with commit rights and no checkpoint. LoopForge turns the informal advice 'keep a human in the loop' into something enforceable, the way a factory line has inspection stations that a part cannot skip. It also lets one vendor's agent write and another's review, a cheap cross-check. It builds on ideas covered earlier: reviewing an agent's plan before it codes (Plannotator, Day 235) and running many agents in parallel (Worktrunk, Day 230). The caveats: it is young software at version 0.3, a self-hosted orchestrator holds powerful repository credentials and must itself be secured, and gates only help if the human at the gate really reads the diff. Also trending: Replit's Missions, which coordinates several agents to plan, build and test toward a stated goal.

Part 1An Anthropic Mathematician Says Claude Helped Prove the Riemann Hypothesis

On November 20 Levent Alpöge, a mathematician on Anthropic's technical staff, posted a four-page note saying he and Claude had proved the Riemann Hypothesis, a 167-year-old conjecture about how prime numbers are spread out and one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems, each worth $1 million. He did not publish a readable proof. Instead he released an archive of roughly 175,000 files written in Lean 4, a language in which a computer checks every logical step, and said the AI-written explanation runs to more than 250,000 pages. Reports say MIT's Andrew Sutherland compiled the code independently, and several number theorists told Nature and Science they suspect it will hold up. But no outside expert has confirmed it, Andrew Granville called the write-up garbled, and Scientific American describes rival claims. Alpöge said he held the news for several days after speaking with Dario Amodei; it landed the day after Anthropic's market debut. One widely shared headline saying mathematicians 'confirm' the proof is not supported by its own article.

The concept, explained simply: A proof assistant such as Lean is a very strict referee. You write each step in a formal language and a small, trusted program checks that every step follows from the rules. If the file compiles, the logic is sound. That still leaves two human jobs. First, someone must check that the statement the computer proved really is the Riemann Hypothesis and not a subtly different sentence, like checking that a contract says what both sides think it says before admiring the signatures. Second, mathematicians want to understand why it is true. A proof that is checked but that nobody can read is like a calculator's answer to a sum you cannot follow: probably right, but it teaches you nothing yet. Why it matters: If it survives, this is the first famous open problem settled mainly by an AI system, and it moves the bottleneck in research from finding proofs to understanding them. If it fails, it will fail in a precise, checkable place, which is itself progress over vague claims. Either way, the habit to copy is the one to use with any AI output: ask what exactly was verified, by what, and who has checked that the question answered is the question asked.

Part 2A Coding Agent Committed a Key, and OpenRouter Cut Three

Yesterday's Dragos canary study (Day 239) now has names attached. On November 21 Together AI reportedly disclosed that an AI coding agent working on its public 'xorl' GitHub repository committed a credential. That credential opened a private Hugging Face repository holding stored samples of customer prompts, and an outsider downloaded samples from four days in June and July for three open models. Together's scanner caught the key and reverted the commit, but too late. The intruder then searched the prompts for other credentials and tried them; five were Dragos canaries. Together has not said how many customers were affected. On November 22 OpenRouter said it had off-boarded three inference providers and removed 125 endpoints from zero-data-retention (ZDR) eligibility, stressing that OpenRouter itself was not breached and that many removals were precautionary. It linked to notices from Novita, Phala and Together AI but did not say these are the three it removed.

The concept, explained simply: Secret scanning is a tool that reads code for things that look like passwords or keys. It can run after code is published (detect and alert) or before (push protection, which blocks the upload). The difference is everything on a public repository, where automated bots copy new commits within seconds. Reverting a commit is like snatching back a postcard after it has gone through the sorting office: the copy exists. The only real fix for a leaked key is to revoke it. And a coding agent treats a credential as just another string unless something in its harness stops it.

Why it matters: This is the first major disclosed leak where the careless committer was an AI agent, and it follows the Fireworks AI breach (Day 228) and the poisoned coding-agent extension (Day 233). The lesson for any team using coding agents: block secrets before the push, give agents short-lived and narrowly scoped credentials, and do not keep customer data behind a single long-lived key. For buyers, 'ZDR eligible' is a label a marketplace can remove overnight, so check which providers actually serve your requests.

Part 3The AI Trade Has Its Worst Week in Years

US markets closed on Friday, November 20 in what NPR called a really bad week for the AI boom. Reports say the S&P 500 fell 3.7% on Friday alone and about 8.6% over the week, the Nasdaq lost about 10% and turned negative for 2026, and both the S&P 500 and the Dow entered a correction. The chip index fell 10.7% and Nvidia closed 13.8% lower after falling on nine of ten sessions. Anthropic's newly listed shares ended roughly 23% below their brief $115.10 peak, which implies a price in the high $80s, close to the IPO price discussed on Day 238. Figures vary between outlets. The causes cited: Nvidia's leadership turmoil (Day 230), doubts about data-centre spending, the Federal Reserve's first rate rise in more than three years in September, and political resistance to new data centres after the midterms. The concept, explained simply: A correction is a fall of 10% or more from a recent high; a bear market is 20%. The deeper worry is interconnection, sometimes called circular financing. Chip makers invest in and lend to AI labs, the labs use the money to buy chips and rent cloud capacity, and cloud firms borrow to build the data centres. It is like a row of shops that are each other's best customers and each other's lenders: when one slows down, all the tills go quiet together. Higher interest rates make every borrowed dollar in that loop more expensive. Why it matters: A share-price fall does not change what the models can do on Monday morning. It can change what vendors charge and how long they survive: cash-burning AI suppliers find funding harder, free tiers shrink and discounts end. If your product depends on a small AI vendor, this is the week to check its runway and your exit plan.

Part 4Governors Ask for Federal AI Rules That Leave State Laws

On November 22 Bloomberg reported that the National Governors Association had set out recommendations for splitting AI regulation between Washington and the states. The federal side would handle frontier-model safety: independent safety reviews of advanced models and mandatory reporting of serious security breaches and safety incidents. States would keep authority over consumer protection, discrimination and AI's effect on jobs. That clashes with the White House, which in March asked Congress to override state AI laws that impose 'undue burdens'. It echoes a September letter from 26 state attorneys general. Analysts expect the fight to resume when the new Congress sits in January. The concept, explained simply: Preemption means a federal law overrides state laws on the same subject. The choice is between a ceiling and a floor. A ceiling says: this is the rule everywhere and states may not add to it, which gives companies one rulebook. A floor says: this is the minimum and states may go further, as with the minimum wage. The governors are asking for a federal floor on frontier safety and no ceiling on everyday harms. Why it matters: For anyone shipping AI products in the US, this decides whether you follow one rulebook or fifty. The likeliest outcome on current evidence is layers: federal duties for the biggest model developers, with state laws on hiring, lending and consumer protection continuing to apply to everyone who deploys AI. Build compliance for the strictest state you sell in.

Part 5UN Talks on Autonomous Weapons End With More Talks

The seventh Review Conference of the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons met in Geneva from November 16 to 20, with Switzerland presiding. The central question was whether to start negotiating a binding instrument on lethal autonomous weapon systems. Campaigners reported that Russia blocked the agenda on the first day; a chair's draft proposed 30 negotiating days and a protocol by 2028, while a US paper backed five more years of non-binding work. News summaries say the conference agreed to keep talking without a firm commitment to restrict such weapons. We could not confirm the final text on UN pages. The concept, explained simply: A lethal autonomous weapon selects and attacks a target without a person making that specific decision. The phrase negotiators argue over is 'meaningful human control': a human who understands the situation, can intervene and is accountable. The forum works by consensus, so every state has a veto, like a committee that can act only when nobody objects. That is why some countries want to move the issue to the UN General Assembly, where a majority vote is enough.

Why it matters: Together with the Call for Control (Day 239) and the Trump-Xi split (Day 237), it shows the same pattern: international AI rules are stuck where big powers disagree. In practice, limits on military AI will come from national policy, procurement contracts and the usage terms of the labs themselves, not from a treaty, for some years.

Market signal

The signal this week is a gap between capability and confidence. On the same weekend that an AI system may have produced the most famous proof in mathematics, AI shares had their worst week in years and a coding agent leaked customer prompts. Capability is no longer the question investors or buyers are asking; cost of capital and trust are. Expect funding to tighten for AI firms that depend on borrowed money, inference marketplaces to compete on audited privacy rather than price, and 'verified' (by a proof checker, a secret scanner or a human gate) to become the word that sells.

Practical takeaways
Ask what was verified, and by what.

For any AI result, separate 'a tool checked the steps' from 'a person confirmed it answers the right question'; you need both.

Block secrets before the push.

Turn on push protection and pre-commit secret scanning in every repository an AI coding agent can write to; alerts after the fact are too late on public code.

Revoke, do not just revert.

When a key leaks, rotate it immediately and assume it was copied; removing the commit does not undo the exposure.

Give agents short-lived, narrow credentials.

Use scoped tokens that expire in hours and open only what the task needs, so one leaked key cannot unlock stored customer data.

Pin your inference providers.

If you use a model router, set an allow-list of providers and recheck their data-retention status this week, since eligibility labels just changed for 125 endpoints.

Check your AI vendors' runway.

After a market correction, ask smaller AI suppliers about funding and pricing plans, and keep a tested fallback model or provider.

Build compliance for the strictest state.

With preemption unsettled, design US AI products to meet the toughest state rules on hiring, lending and consumer protection.

Put a human gate before anything ships.

Make agent-written code pass tests, a second reviewer and a named person's approval before merge, and make the gate impossible to skip.

Self-test
What does it mean that the claimed Riemann proof is 'checked in Lean', and what does that not settle?

A computer has confirmed every logical step follows the rules; it does not settle whether the formal statement truly is the Riemann Hypothesis or give humans an understanding of why it is true.

Why did reverting the commit not protect Together AI's customers?

On a public repository a leaked key can be copied within seconds, so the credential was used to download prompt samples before the revert; only revoking the key ends the risk.

What is the difference between a correction and a bear market?

A correction is a fall of 10% or more from a recent high; a bear market is a fall of 20% or more.

What is circular financing in the AI sector?

Chip makers and cloud firms invest in or lend to AI labs that then spend the money on their chips and capacity, so trouble at one company spreads to the others.

In preemption terms, what is the difference between a floor and a ceiling?

A floor sets a federal minimum that states may exceed; a ceiling sets one national rule and bars states from adding their own.

What does a human approval gate do in a LoopForge workflow?

It pauses the run at a set step until a person approves it or sends the work back to an earlier step.

What we're watching

Whether the Lean and Mathlib communities or named number theorists confirm that the formal statement in Alpöge's archive is the Riemann Hypothesis. item.title: Fake Passwords Expose Leaky AI Providers, Congress Reveals 900,000 Approved Chips for China, and Walmart Lets Shopping Agents In Before Black Friday
item.dc:creator: Varun Singla
item.description: Dragos's two-million-prompt canary experiment, the House committee's export-licence disclosure, the SEC's Nvidia probe and its insurance gap, Walmart's Agent Gateway for outside AI agents, a growing coalition calling…
item.content:encoded:
Dragos's two-million-prompt canary experiment, the House committee's export-licence disclosure, the SEC's Nvidia probe and its insurance gap, Walmart's Agent Gateway for outside AI agents, a growing coalition calling for control of frontier models, and CLI-Anything, the repo turning desktop software into agent tools.

Viral / open-source spotlight

CLI-Anything: turning desktop software into tools an agent can drive

CLI-Anything (github.com/HKUDS/CLI-Anything), from the Data Intelligence Lab at the University of Hong Kong, appeared on November 21 AI trend lists with about 770 new stars, under the slogan 'Making ALL Software Agent-Native'. It is mainly a plugin for coding agents such as Claude Code (installed with /plugin marketplace add HKUDS/CLI-Anything); you point it at a program that has source code and it generates a full command-line interface for it, plus a skill file the agent can read. Ready-made CLIs exist for GIMP, Blender, LibreOffice, 3D-printing files and cloud APIs, and an arXiv paper, 'CLI-Anything: Towards Agent-Native Computer Use', describes the method and a sharing hub called CLI-Hub. Why it is taking off: Yesterday's issue covered computer-use agents that look at the screen and click like a person (Apple's agent, Day 238). That works for any app but is slow, costly and fragile: a moved button breaks it. CLI-Anything takes the other road. A command like 'blender render --scene intro --frames 1-120' is exact, fast, cheap in tokens and easy to check, and agents are already excellent at the terminal. Think of it as giving the agent a remote control with labelled buttons instead of asking it to operate the TV by looking at it. The caveats: it only works where the source code is available, a generated CLI can miss features or get them wrong, and a command line with full access to your files deserves the same permissions caution as any agent. Also trending: minimind (about 850 stars in a day), which trains a 64-million-parameter language model from scratch in about two hours on one GPU, a hands-on way to learn how LLMs are built.

Part 1Two Million Fake Secrets Show Where AI Prompts Leak

Researchers at the industrial-security firm Dragos, led by chief research officer HD Moore, published a study titled 'Three breaches, endless leaks'. From July to November 2026 they sent about two million prompts to widely used AI services. Each prompt contained a unique, trackable fake secret: a URL, a password or a set of AWS keys that led to nothing real. Then they watched for anyone trying to use them. Some did. The team reports signs that data from at least three AI providers was exposed: planted credentials were tried against their test systems and decoy AWS accounts. In one case, secrets sent to two different providers were used together, almost immediately, from a single rented server, which suggests one attacker was inside both. Separately, resellers on an AI inference marketplace could see and keep customer prompts through ordinary logging, without hacking anything, and some prompts sent to US providers ended up with Chinese AI organisations. Some stolen requests were flagged 'zero data retention'. The concept, explained simply: A canary token (or honeytoken) is bait. You plant a fake secret that no honest process would ever use, so any attempt to use it is proof that someone saw it who should not have. It works like dye packs in bank cash: it does not stop the theft, but it tells you it happened and roughly where. The study also shows the 'fourth-party' problem. When you use an AI app, your prompt may pass from the app to a router or marketplace, then to a reseller, then to the company actually running the model. Each hop can log it. A 'zero data retention' flag is a promise about what a provider stores, not a guarantee against an attacker or a careless reseller in the chain. Why it matters: This is the first large, measured look at what happens to prompts after you press Enter, and it follows this month's Fireworks AI breach (Days 228 and 233). Anyone pasting API keys, customer data or internal links into AI tools should assume a leak is possible somewhere along the chain. The cheap fix is to keep secrets out of prompts, use short-lived credentials, and plant your own canaries in places agents can read, so you find out fast.

Part 2Congress Reveals 900,000 AI Chips Approved for China

On November 19 the House Foreign Affairs Committee, chaired by Brian Mast, released export-licence records showing the administration approved sales of roughly 900,000 advanced AI chips, Nvidia H200s and AMD MI325Xs, to Chinese companies between December 2025 and May

Part 3An SEC Probe Into Nvidia, and an Insurance Gap

The Wall Street Journal reported on November 17 that the Securities and Exchange Commission has opened a civil investigation into whether Nvidia's disclosures misled investors. Neither side has confirmed it, the SEC says it does not comment, and no enforcement action has been announced. Reports link it to Jensen Huang's departure (Day 230) and to Nvidia's decision last year to stop breaking out sales to Singapore, a hub through which chips can reach other countries. A Reuters analysis added that Nvidia's directors and officers are insured for up to $950 million, but the company lacks the insurance that would normally cover its own legal costs and settlements in securities lawsuits. Nvidia paid $5.5 million in 2022 to settle SEC charges over crypto-mining sales. The concept, explained simply: Directors-and-officers (D&O) insurance usually has three parts. 'Side A' pays individual directors when the company cannot. 'Side B' repays the company when it covers its directors. 'Side C', or entity coverage, pays the company's own costs when the company itself is sued over its securities. Some very large firms skip Side C because it is expensive and they can afford to pay out of their own pocket. An investigation does not mean wrongdoing; it is a fact-finding stage that often ends with no action. Why it matters: The world's most valuable chip maker now faces a leadership change, a federal probe and lawsuits without entity insurance, all at once. Disclosure questions, such as where chips really end up, are becoming governance questions for the whole AI supply chain. If your strategy depends on Nvidia supply, nothing changes this week, but a long investigation can distract management in the middle of a product cycle.

Part 4Walmart Opens a Door for Outside Shopping Agents

With Black Friday on November 27, Walmart's Agent Gateway is the clearest example of a big retailer inviting AI agents in rather than blocking them. Announced on October 21 and now in early beta for approved developers, it is an MCP server that lets outside agents, such as ChatGPT, Gemini and Meta's Muse, shop at Walmart and Sam's Club. They do not touch the catalogue or checkout directly: they talk to Sparky, Walmart's own assistant, which does the work. Outside agents never see card numbers or full order histories, customers approve purchases by default, shoppers can set spending limits such as $50 or $100, and Walmart may ask for extra approval even within a limit. Walmart says Sparky users spend about 35-40% more per order. The contrast is Amazon, which blocks outside agents.

The concept, explained simply: This is agent-to-agent commerce. Your agent (the buyer's representative) talks to the store's agent (the seller's representative), much as two lawyers talk for their clients. The store keeps control of prices, stock and payment, and shares only what the task needs. MCP, the Model Context Protocol (see the March MCP deep dive), is the standard plug that lets the two connect. A spending limit plus an approval step is the agent version of a corporate card with a manager sign-off.

Why it matters: Two models of the agent web are forming: open doors with house rules (Walmart, Cloudflare's agent browser on Day 232) and walled gardens (Amazon, sites locking out agents on Day 230). For businesses, it is time to decide which you are. For shoppers, the safest setup this holiday season is a low spending limit and approval for every purchase.

Part 5More Countries Join the Call to Control Frontier AI

The 'Call for Control of Frontier AI Models', launched on September 21 at the UN General Assembly by about 20 countries and the European Commission, keeps gaining signatures. Newsletter roundups this week put the count at 32 states plus the Commission, a figure we could not confirm on official pages, and the President of Finland and the Prime Minister of Norway have issued a joint statement on next steps, saying more countries have joined. The call asks for mandatory testing of frontier models before release and suggests a new international body to set standards, check compliance and convene states when AI capabilities cross agreed thresholds. The United States and China have not signed.

The concept, explained simply: A capability threshold is a pre-agreed line, for example 'a model can meaningfully help build a cyber weapon' or 'a model can improve itself without humans'. Crossing it triggers an agreed response, such as extra testing, restricted release or an international meeting, like an alarm level in a nuclear plant. Pre-release testing means outside evaluators examine a model before the public gets it, rather than after problems appear. Why it matters: Without the two biggest AI powers, the call cannot bind the labs that matter most. But it creates a shared vocabulary and a ready-made structure. If a serious incident happens, governments will reach for exactly this kind of plan, and the EU AI Act's rules for general-purpose models already point the same way.

Market signal

This week's signal is about trust in the plumbing, not new models. Prompts leak through reseller chains, chip licences turn out to be paper rather than shipments, the biggest chip maker faces questions about its own disclosures, and retailers are writing the rules for agents that spend money. The money keeps flowing (record IPO, record leases), but buyers are starting to price the cost of verifying what vendors say. Expect contracts to ask more about subprocessors, audit rights and agent permissions, and expect vendors that can prove where data and chips go to win deals.

Practical takeaways
Keep secrets out of prompts.

Never paste API keys, passwords or private links into an AI tool; use a secrets manager and short-lived tokens that agents fetch when needed.

Plant your own canaries.

Put a few fake credentials in documents and folders your AI agents can read, and set alerts so you know within minutes if one is ever used.

Map your fourth parties.

Ask each AI vendor which routers, resellers and inference providers actually process your prompts, and get it in the contract.

Read export news by shipments, not approvals.

When judging chip supply or China risk, look for shipped and delivered figures; licence approvals overstate what moves.

Check your vendors' governance, not just their products.

For critical AI suppliers, note open investigations, leadership changes and legal exposure as part of vendor risk reviews.

Set spending limits before letting agents shop.

If you try agent shopping this Black Friday, use a low cap, require approval for every order, and use a card you can freeze.

Decide your agent-access policy.

If you run a website or store, choose whether outside agents get an official door with rules or are blocked, rather than leaving it to chance.

Prefer structured tools over screen-clicking.

Where an app has a CLI or API, give agents that instead of computer-use control; it is faster, cheaper and easier to audit.

Self-test
What is a canary token, and what did Dragos use it for?

A fake secret that no honest process would use, so any use proves exposure; Dragos planted them in about two million prompts to see which AI providers' data leaked.

Why does a 'zero data retention' flag not fully protect a prompt?

It is a storage promise by one provider; resellers, routers or an attacker already inside the chain can still see and keep the prompt.

What is the difference between an approved export licence and a shipped chip?

A licence is permission to sell; the chip still has to be shipped and allowed into the buyer's country, and most of the roughly 900,000 approved chips reportedly never moved.

What does 'Side C' D&O insurance cover, and why does it matter for Nvidia?

Entity coverage pays a company's own costs in securities claims; Nvidia reportedly lacks it, so it would pay defence and settlements itself.

How do outside agents shop at Walmart through the Agent Gateway?

They connect over MCP to Walmart's own agent, Sparky, which handles catalogue and checkout; card data stays hidden and customers approve purchases within set limits.

Why is a CLI often better for agents than screen-based computer use?

Commands are exact, fast, cheap in tokens and easy to verify, while clicking on screens is slow and breaks when the layout changes.

What we're watching

Whether ANT holds above its $83 IPO price when markets reopen on Monday, November 23. What We're Watching: Whether any AI provider named or implicated in the Dragos study confirms a breach or changes its reseller rules. What We're Watching: Votes on the AI OVERWATCH Act and any new figures on how many approved chips actually shipped to China. What We're Watching: Wells Fargo's AI-agent liability terms taking effect on November 24, and Black Friday data on agent-driven shopping. What We're Watching: Further signatures to the Call for Control of Frontier AI Models and any official update on the 32-country figure.

Sources. dragos.com/blog/ai-supply-chain-security-canary-tokens, labs.cloudsecurityalliance.org and unit42.paloaltonetworks.com (prompt leaks, inference-provider risk); thestandard.com.hk, unite.ai, tomshardware.com and introl.com (900,000 chip licences, AI OVERWATCH Act); investmentnews.com, pymnts.com, tweaktown.com and cryptobriefing.com (SEC Nvidia probe, insurance); techcrunch.com, techstrong.ai, ppc.land, letsdatascience.com and retaildive.com (Walmart Agent Gateway and Sparky); government.nl, regjeringen.no, aljazeera.com and thenextweb.com (Call for Control of Frontier AI Models); github.com/HKUDS/CLI-Anything, arxiv.org/abs/2606.03854 and github.com/duanyytop/agents-radar (CLI-Anything, minimind); newsletter roundups for November 21. Figures are secondary reports and unverified unless from the company's own page or filing.

item.title: Anthropic Slides Toward Its IPO Price on Day Two, an Open-Source AI Hacking Kit Knocks Out EU Payroll, and Apple Starts Building an Agent to Run Your Mac
item.dc:creator: Varun Singla
item.description: ANT falls about 10% to near $87 as the greenshoe lifts the raise to $93.5 billion, the European Commission confirms attackers used the ARTEX agent framework, a job listing shows Apple building a computer-use agent while…
item.content:encoded:
ANT falls about 10% to near $87 as the greenshoe lifts the raise to $93.5 billion, the European Commission confirms attackers used the ARTEX agent framework, a job listing shows Apple building a computer-use agent while macOS makes rivals harder to enable, Riot names Anthropic as the tenant of a $28 billion, 910 MW Texas campus, and Linger is the local personal agent developers are starring.

Viral / open-source spotlight

Linger: a personal agent that runs a large model on an ordinary PC

Linger (github.com/simplexai-labs/linger) appeared on November 20 GitHub trend lists as 'an open-source personal agent that runs fully on your PC'. It is a desktop app for Apple-silicon Macs (macOS 14+), Windows and Linux that connects to your mail, chats, calendar and browser, builds a shared memory from them, and assembles small agent teams for tasks such as finding flights and hotels; actions like sending an email wait for your approval. Its headline claim is local inference: its PolyStrata engine runs a 125-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model (Qwen3.8-Flash-Next) on a 12 GB RTX 3060 with 64 GB of RAM at about 45 tokens per second, with a 'Model Autopilot' installer that detects your hardware and picks the best model that fits. There are no token fees because nothing is sent to a cloud model. Why it is taking off: It speaks to two worries at once: cost (cloud agents can burn through tokens) and privacy (this week's reports about agents leaking data). The technical trick is worth understanding. A mixture-of-experts model has many 'expert' sub-networks but uses only a few for each word, so Linger keeps the most-used experts on the graphics card, the occasionally used ones in ordinary RAM and the rarely used ones on the SSD, moving them up as they get busy, a memory hierarchy like a CPU cache. The caveats: the speed and 'Claude-class' quality claims are the project's own, heavily compressed (2-bit) models lose some accuracy, the macOS build is not yet signed, and an agent with access to your mail and browser deserves the same caution as any cloud one. Try it on a spare machine with test accounts first.

Part 1Anthropic's Second Day: Down About 10%, Five Cents From Its IPO Price

A day after closing its debut at $97.17 (Day 237), Anthropic's stock fell about 10% on November 20 US time, to roughly $87.25 (some outlets quote a close of $88.30, down 9.1%). At its low it came within about five cents of the $83 IPO price. The fall came in a wider sell-off in AI and tech shares. At the same time the underwriters fully exercised their greenshoe option: 147 million extra shares, exactly 15% of the 980 million offered, which takes the deal to 1.127 billion shares and about $93.5 billion in gross proceeds. Add the separate $26 billion private placement and outlets put the total raised at about $119.5 billion. Commentators noted that Facebook and Uber each lost about 11% on their second trading days.

The concept, explained simply: A greenshoe (over-allotment option) lets the banks sell up to 15% more shares than the deal's headline size. They sell the extra shares on day one, which leaves them 'short'. If the price falls below the IPO price, they buy shares back in the market to cover that short, and that buying acts as a cushion that supports the price; this is called price stabilisation. If the price stays above the IPO price, buying back would lose money, so instead they exercise the option and take the extra shares from the company at the IPO price. A full exercise means the banks did not need to buy shares back to support the stock: it had stayed above $83. There is also a 'liquidity drain' effect: a deal this large pulls money out of other stocks, because investors sell what they own to pay for the new shares. Why it matters: Day two shows how quickly first-day excitement can fade, and how a record-sized listing interacts with the rest of the market. For anyone who relies on Anthropic, this is a reminder that its share price will now swing with sector moods unrelated to its products. The real test is the first quarterly report as a public company, not the first week's trading. If ANT ever trades below $83, the banks' stabilisation cushion is already used up, because the greenshoe was exercised.

Part 2An Open-Source AI Attack Kit Knocks EU Staff Systems Offline

On November 19 the European Commission confirmed that attackers used an AI tool in a cyberattack on its internal systems. First signs were detected on October 22, and CERT-EU reportedly identified the tool as ARTEX. Payroll, leave requests, medical reimbursements, timesheets and translation services were disrupted for more than ten days; most systems are back, though one report says payroll failed again after being restored. The Commission says it has no evidence of a broad breach of staff data and knows of no ransom demand, while Politico reported that large amounts of personal data may have been exposed. A week earlier, on November 13, the FBI issued a FLASH alert warning that criminal and state-aligned groups have used ARTEX since at least August against finance, government, technology, defence and healthcare targets, with some intrusions going from first contact to privileged access in under three hours. ARTEX was published on GitHub in July and removed on October 8, but copies and a paid 'ARTEX PRO' edition still circulate.

The concept, explained simply: ARTEX is a multi-agent penetration-testing framework: software that strings AI agents together to do the steps a human hacker would, such as mapping a network, finding weak points, trying exploits and moving to more powerful accounts. It has no model of its own; it plugs into whatever commercial or open model the attacker connects. Defenders talk about 'dwell time' (how long an attacker is inside before being caught) and 'breakout time' (how long from first foothold to spreading further). Agents shrink both, because they work at machine speed and never get tired. The same tools are legitimately used by security teams to test their own systems, which is why they are hard to ban: the difference is permission, not code. Why it matters: This is one of the first confirmed cases of a major government body being disrupted by an AI-driven attack tool, and it fits the trend seen with OpenAI's 'Critical for cyber' rating (Day 236) and the agent-security deals (Days 228 and 237). The lesson for organisations is that monitoring and response must work at the same speed: alerts that a human reviews the next morning are too slow when an intrusion can finish in three hours. Removing a repository from GitHub also did little; once an attack tool is open-sourced, it stays available.

Part 3Apple Is Building an Agent to Run Your Mac, and Raising Walls for Rivals

A job listing first reported by Bloomberg, and covered by TechCrunch on November 19, shows Apple hiring a senior engineering manager to lead work on an 'AI agent that can use a computer'. The listing describes agents that move 'fluidly between tools' and carry out multi-step tasks across apps, browsers, command lines, code and APIs, including writing and fixing their own code. Bloomberg reports Apple has looked at launching as soon as the end of next year, and that the work is early; the listing has since been removed. At the same time, the macOS 27.3 beta adds warning screens asking users to reconsider before giving third-party agents control of their Mac, and enabling ChatGPT's computer-use mode reportedly now takes 14 steps instead of four. ChatGPT, Gemini and Meta's Muse can already operate a Mac this way.

The concept, explained simply: A computer-use agent works a computer the way a person does: it looks at the screen (through screenshots or the accessibility system that screen readers use), decides what to click or type, does it, and checks the result, in a loop. To do this on a Mac, an outside app needs powerful permissions such as Accessibility and Screen Recording, which is exactly where Apple can add friction. The company that owns the operating system is the platform gatekeeper: it decides how easy it is for others to control the device. A built-in agent can be given deeper, safer access (for example through app 'intents' that expose actions directly) while rivals must go through the slower screen-reading route.

Why it matters: The agent race is moving from chat windows to the operating system, and the OS owners (Apple, Microsoft with Copilot, Day 235, and Google) hold a structural advantage. Extra warning screens can be defended as security, since an agent with full control of your Mac is a large risk (see Meta's Muse privacy reports this week), but they also shape competition and may draw regulators' attention, especially in the EU. For users and IT teams, expect a choice between a tightly integrated built-in agent and more capable but harder-to-enable third-party ones.

Part 4Riot Names Anthropic as the Tenant of a $28 Billion Texas AI Campus

Riot Platforms, best known as a bitcoin miner, used its quarterly filing on November 18 to confirm that the 'frontier AI lab' leasing its entire Corsicana, Texas campus is Anthropic. The 15-year lease covers 910 megawatts and is worth about $28 billion in rent over the initial term (about $1.8 billion a year), rising to about $54 billion if both five-year extensions are used. It became binding on November 4. Riot must fund roughly $5.5 billion of development and may reimburse Anthropic up to about $3.6 billion for its data-centre modules; if a phase is more than 270 days late, Anthropic can cancel that phase. Anthropic also leases 191 MW at Riot's Rockdale site, so it takes 1,101 of Riot's 1,151 MW of contracted capacity.

The concept, explained simply: AI data centres are now priced in megawatts of power, not square metres of floor space, because electricity and grid connections are the scarcest input. Bitcoin miners already own sites with big grid connections, cooling and permits ('powered land'), which is why many are turning into AI landlords. In a 'powered shell' deal like this, the landlord provides the building, power and cooling, and the tenant brings and runs the computers. A rough rule: 1 gigawatt can run hundreds of thousands of modern AI chips, so 910 MW is a frontier-scale training and inference site. Delivery deadlines with cancellation rights show who holds power in the deal: the tenant with the money. Why it matters: It shows where part of Anthropic's IPO money is going: long, fixed commitments for power and buildings that will need years of revenue growth to pay for. Concentration cuts both ways: Riot now depends on one customer for almost all its contracted capacity, and Anthropic depends on Riot delivering on time. Combined with Nvidia saying it has stopped shipping licensed chips to China (its guidance now assumes no China data-centre revenue), the picture is of compute being built out fast in the US while the supply map splits along political lines.

Market signal

Anthropic gave back most of its first-day gain within 24 hours even as its banks sold 15% more stock, while the same week brought a $28 billion power-and-buildings commitment in Texas. Nvidia's guidance now assumes zero China data-centre sales, and an open-source attack framework disrupted a major government body. The signal: money for AI capacity is still flowing at record scale, but public investors are pricing in volatility and the security bill is rising alongside the compute bill. Plan for cheaper models, more expensive defence, and vendors whose share prices move with the sector rather than their own news.

Practical takeaways
Do not read a stock's first week as a verdict.

Judge AI vendors on reliability, pricing and quarterly results; first-week swings mostly reflect supply and sector mood.

Check that your detection works in hours, not days.

Test whether an intrusion that reaches admin rights in three hours would trigger an alert someone acts on the same day.

Run authorised AI red-team tests on yourself.

Use agent-based testing tools with written permission, so you find the weak points before an ARTEX-style attacker does.

Protect payroll and HR as critical systems.

The EU attack hit staff pay first; make sure these back-office systems have backups, offline copies and a tested recovery plan.

Audit which agents can control your computers.

List every app with Accessibility, Screen Recording or full-disk access on company Macs and PCs, and remove what is not needed.

Plan for built-in OS agents.

Assume Apple, Microsoft and Google will ship deeply integrated agents; decide your policy for them before they arrive, not after.

Ask your AI providers where their compute comes from.

Long leases with delivery deadlines can slip; ask about capacity plans, regions and what happens if a site is late.

Try a local model for private tasks.

Test a local agent such as Linger on non-sensitive data and compare its quality and speed with your cloud model before trusting it with real accounts.

Self-test
What is a greenshoe option, and what does a full exercise tell you?

It lets IPO banks sell up to 15% extra shares and either buy them back to support the price or take them from the company at the IPO price; a full exercise means the stock stayed above the IPO price, so no stabilising buy-back was needed.

How much did Anthropic's IPO raise after the greenshoe?

About $93.5 billion from 1.127 billion shares, or about $119.5 billion including the $26 billion private placement.

What is ARTEX and why is it hard to stop?

An open-source multi-agent penetration-testing framework that plugs into any LLM; it was removed from GitHub but copies and a paid edition still circulate, and similar tools are used legitimately by defenders.

What is a computer-use agent?

An AI that operates a computer like a person, looking at the screen, clicking and typing in a loop, which needs powerful permissions the OS owner can control.

Why are bitcoin miners becoming AI landlords?

They already own 'powered land': sites with large grid connections, cooling and permits, and power is now the scarcest input for AI data centres.

How does Linger run a 125B model on a 12 GB GPU?

It uses a mixture-of-experts model and keeps the busiest experts on the GPU, others in RAM and rarely used ones on the SSD, moving them as demand changes.

What we're watching

Whether ANT holds above its $83 IPO price as the AI sell-off continues into next week. What We're Watching: Any update from the European Commission or Politico on whether staff personal data was exposed in the ARTEX attack. What We're Watching: Wells Fargo's AI-agent liability terms taking effect on November 24, and whether other banks follow. What We're Watching: Reaction from OpenAI, Google and regulators to Apple's tighter macOS rules for third-party computer-use agents. What We're Watching: Whether the US and China publish final terms for the AI incident notification channel discussed in Shenzhen.

Sources. kucoin.com, thenextweb.com, cryptobriefing.com, mlq.ai, trendingtopics.eu and ceoeconomy.com (Anthropic day two and greenshoe); therecord.media, cryptonomist.ch, beinsure.com, newsweek.com, bleepingcomputer.com, blackfog.com and letsdatascience.com (European Commission attack, FBI ARTEX alert); techcrunch.com, betanews.com, digitaltrends.com and ceoeconomy.com (Apple agent); baxtel.com, aiweekly.co, w.media and bitcoinmagazine.com (Riot-Anthropic lease); bloomberg.com, businessday.co.za and bworldonline.com (Nvidia China halt); github.com/simplexai-labs/linger, trendshift.io and github.com/raiscui/gh-trends (Linger); ctvnews.ca and futurism.com (Meta Muse privacy); creati.ai and theneuron.ai (daily digests). Figures are secondary reports and unverified unless from the company's own page or filing.
